title.en: Ndengei, the Serpent in the Cave of Nakauvadra
title.zh: 納夸瓦德拉洞中蛇神恩登蓋

region.en: Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, Viti Levu, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島拉基拉基上方考萬德拉山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908, ch. on religion

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth'

summary.en: Ndengei is supreme among the Kalou-vu, the original gods; in serpent form he lies coiled in a cavern in the Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, and when he turns himself the earth quakes. Priests crawl to his cave-mouth with hundreds of hogs and turtle and come out holding yam, dripping with rain, or flinging fire-brands; in some versions he has only the head and neck of a serpent, the rest of his body being stone. He is the creator of mankind, with no emotion but hunger — and his son Rokomautu scraped the land up from the ocean bed and taught men how to produce fire.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋為原初神（Kalou-vu）之首，全維提島及外島皆奉其號令。蛇形之軀盤踞於拉基拉基上方考萬德拉山的岩洞之中；他一翻身，大地便震動。拉基拉基人以數百頭豬與海龜獻於洞口，祭司跪爬至洞前進洞請願：求芋豐收則捧芋而出，求雨則滴水而歸，求戰勝則有火把擲出、兵器交擊之聲應殺敵之數。有的版本說他只有蛇頭蛇頸，身軀皆石。他造人類，卻無喜無怒，唯飢而已。其子羅科馬烏圖自海底刮起陸地：衣裾拖過處成沙灘，衣裾撩起處成石岸；又教人取火之術。

sensitivity.note: Colonial administrator-anthropologist record (Thomson 1908); iTaukei heritage. Thomson argues Ndengei is Melanesian, not Polynesian.

passages.text: Ndengei is supreme among the Kalou-vu (original gods), and his authority was recognized by the whole of Vitilevu and its outlying islands, and by the western half of Vanua-levu. The oldest tradition in which his name occurs mentions him as one of the first immigrants with Lutu-na-somba-somba, but his fame far exceeded that of his companions, and so many myths gathered about his name, that when the first missionaries arrived he had come to be a counterpart of Zeus himself. In serpent form he lay coiled in a cavern in the Kauvandra mountain above Rakiraki, and when he turned himself the earth quaked. Enormous offerings of food were made to him by the Rakiraki people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

passages.text: Several hundred hogs and turtle were carried to the mouth of the cavern, which the priests approached, crawling on their knees and elbows. One of the priests then entered the cave to proffer the request. If it was for a good yam-crop he would reappear, holding a piece of yam which the god had given him; if for rain, he would be dripping with water; if for victory, a fire-brand would be flung out in token that the enemy would be consumed, or a clashing of clubs would be heard, one for each of the enemy that would be slaughtered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

passages.text: Beyond the limits of his own district he had scarcely a temple, and little actual worship was paid to him, though in the great drought of 1838 King Tanoa of Mbau sent propitiatory offerings to him. In some versions Ndengei has the head and neck only of a serpent, the rest of his body being of stone. He is the creator of mankind, but he has no emotions, sensations, or appetites except hunger. Another version describes him as sending forth his son, Rokomautu, to create the land. He scraped it up from the ocean-bed, and where his flowing garment trailed across it there were sandy beaches, and where the skirt was looped up the coast was rocky. He also taught men how to produce fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908); not verbatim.

title.en: The Shooting of Turukawa, Ndengei's Awakener

region.en: Kauvandra mountain, Viti Levu, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟維提島考萬德拉山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908 (version of Ilai Motonithothoko)

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth — The Shooting of the Sacred Pigeon'

summary.en: The twin grand-nephews of Ndengei tamed a pigeon, Turukawa, whose cooing at sunrise roused the somnolent old god; a messenger carried it off on the father's assurance, and when the twins found their bird in Ndengei's village they shot it with the bow called Summer-lightning and fortified themselves with Rokola's carpenters. There was war in Kauvandra such as Fiji has never seen since — and a vine-bridge snare that swung Ndengei's warriors into the fortress to be clubbed at leisure.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋的兩個孫侄輩雙生子馴得一隻鴿子，取名圖魯卡瓦；晨昏潮汐，鴿鳴遠播——老人恩登蓋嗜睡，全靠這鴿子喚醒。使者趁兄弟外出，憑其父一句『不必他們同意』把鴿子取走。雙子聞鴿鳴於神村，大怒：『這就是你們對待人類子孫的方式嗎？』遂以名喚『夏之閃電』的弓射殺神鴿，並入羅科拉的木匠村，倚其戰柵自固。考萬德拉山由此爆發斐濟史上從未有過的大戰：恩登蓋與羅科穆托的聯軍圍攻韋西木戰柵，屢攻不克；羅科拉更設毒計——在裂谷上張藤橋，橋畔暗設鴨網式的繩套，敵兵一踏上便被高吊入堡，任憑處置。恩登蓋軍心大沮。

sensitivity.note: Record of a native-written version (Ilai Motonithothoko) via Thomson 1908; iTaukei heritage.

passages.text: When Ndengei had grown old the settlement on the Kauvandra mountain consisted of several villages, one of which belonged to Rokola and his carpenter clan, and the grandsons of the first arrivals were grown men. In the village of Nai-lango-nawanawa, on the slopes of the mountain, lived two twin grand-nephews of Ndengei, named Na-thiri-kau-moli and Na-kau-sambaria, who having brought down a pigeon with an arrow without injuring it, clipped its wings and tamed it. They gave the bird the name of Turukawa, and every morning and evening, and at flood-tide and ebb-tide, its cooing resounded far and wide over the mountain. Old Ndengei, hearing its voice, sent a messenger to ask the youths to give it to him, but they were absent from home, and the messenger, assured by their father that their consent was not necessary, took the bird to his master. Ndengei wanted the bird for a practical purpose. Elderly Fijians are somnolent, and the pigeon's cooing at sunrise was useful in arousing him from slumber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the twin brothers were startled at hearing their pigeon cooing in Ndengei's village, and when they heard that it had been taken away without their consent, they flew into a rage, crying, 'Sombo! is this to be the way with us children of men?' And they made ready their bow, which was called Livaliva-ni-singa (Summer-lightning), and set forth to shoot Turukawa. And when they drew near the banyan-tree in which he was perched, they doffed their turbans; therefore the place is called Ai-thavu-thavu-ni-sala (the Doffing-place) to this day. And they shot an arrow at Turukawa, who fell dead to the ground. And they drew out the arrow, and went to the carpenters' village, Narauyamba, because it was fortified, and their own village was not fortified. For four days Ndengei missed the cooing of his Awakener, and he sent Uto, his messenger, to see what had become of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Uto came to the banyan-tree, and found the body of Turukawa, and saw the arrow-wound, and said, 'There is none who would so forget Ndengei as to kill his Awakener but the twin brothers whose bird he was.' Then Ndengei sent to them to come to him, and they refused. And his anger blazed up within him, and he cried with a terrible voice, 'Go, tell them to depart to a land where I am not known!' But this also they refused to do, and Rokola ordered his carpenters to build a war-fence of vesi timber, very high, with neither joint nor chink in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then there was war in Kauvandra — such a war as has never since been seen in Fiji. Joined to Ndengei were Rokomouto and his clan, who had settled on Viwa, and together they laid siege to the fortress. Many heroes fell on either side, but never a warrior could storm the wall of vesi built by the carpenters. But now Rokola devised a dreadful engine of war. Before the gate of his fortress there was a ragged rift in the mountain-side. He sent out his warriors to cut stout vines in the forest, and suspended a bridge of twisted vines over the chasm. From the tops of two stout posts, planted within the fortress, he stretched ropes that appeared to be mere supports to the bridge, but were in reality a trap such as the men of Notho use when they would snare wild duck in their taro-beds. For when a man trod upon them he was caught fast in a noose, and the defenders hauled suddenly upon the ropes, and swung him high over the rampart into their midst, where they could club him at leisure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

title.en: The Deluge of the Vungayali-Tree and the Lifeboat
title.zh: 武恩加亞利樹之洪與救命舟

region.en: Kauvandra to the western ocean, Fiji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斐濟考萬德拉至西海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Basil Thomson, The Fijians, 1908 (version of Ilai Motonithothoko)

source.work: Basil Thomson, The Fijians: A Study of the Decay of Custom (London: Heinemann, 1908), 'The Ndengei Myth — The Great Deluge'

summary.en: When Ndengei could not take the fortress by force, a traitor's dream told him to cut the vungayali-tree by the rampart: water gushed from the wound, flooded the fortress knee-deep by nightfall, and became a river flowing south. The carpenters built canoes in haste and sailed to a new land — the ancestors of the carpenter clan at Rewa — while the twin brothers, for Rokola's sake, were given time to build the Nai-vaka-nawanawa, the Lifeboat, 'a vessel such as has never since been seen in Fiji,' and sailed into the western ocean, never heard of more.
summary.zh: 恩登蓋力攻不下，便尋得與木匠同族卻為己方效力的叛徒姆巴坎德羅蒂，命他獻計破敵。當夜神靈入夢，教他砍伐戰柵旁那株 vungayali 樹。斧落樹根，泉水噴涌而出——整日灌入堡中，入夜已深及膝，且仍在漲。木匠們商議，既神明相助，不如乞和；恩登蓋與眾酋議定：『這批工匠太有用，不可殺，改判流放！』泉水已成南流的大河，木匠們倉促造舟，順流而下，至新陸定居——這便是雷瓦木匠氏族的祖先。至於雙生子，罪無可赦，本應終身放逐；但看在羅科拉的情面，准其造舟自贖。羅科拉為他們造出一艘斐濟空前的巨舟，命名『納伊瓦卡納瓦納瓦』——救命舟；兄弟二人順流入西海而去，從此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Record of a native-written version via Thomson 1908; iTaukei heritage. Flood cluster; cross-ref melanesian-dengei-flood-canoe-builders (Fison recension).

passages.text: There were traitors in Ndengei's camp, who were conspiring with the enemy, and carrying food to him by night. These men were seized, and being found guilty on their own confession, were exiled from Kauvandra for ever. Now, when Ndengei saw that he could not prevail against the fortress, he sought out one Mbakandroti, a man related to the carpenters, who had chosen to take part with Ndengei against his own kin, and bade him devise a plan for betraying the fortress. That night a spirit appeared to Mbakandroti in a dream, and told him to cut down a vungayali-tree that grew close to the rampart. And when he had related his dream, one Vueti was appointed to cut it down. He had scarce laid his stone axe to the root when water began to gush forth from the wound. All that day the water poured into the fortress, and by nightfall it was knee-deep, and rising still. So the carpenters took counsel, and resolved to ask pardon of Ndengei, since the gods were with him. So Ndengei took counsel with his chiefs, and they said, 'These craftsmen are too valuable; we cannot destroy them; let them be exiled!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

passages.text: The fountain had now become a mighty river flowing southward from the mountain, and the craftsmen built them canoes in haste, and embarked, and sailed down the stream till they came to a new land, and there they settled. These are the ancestors of the carpenter clan at Rewa. But there was no pardon for the twin brothers; to their exile there was to be no limit. Yet, for Rokola's sake, they were given time to build their canoe. And Rokola built them a vessel such as has never since been seen in Fiji, and named it Nai-vaka-nawanawa (the Lifeboat), and sailed away down the stream into the western ocean, and were never heard of more; only the prophecy remains that when they reappear on earth the power of Ndengei, which is the Old Serpent, would continue in the ascendant, for the twins were gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Thomson, The Fijians, 'The Ndengei Myth' (1908), version of Ilai Motonithothoko; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the Tagai Constellation

region.zh: 托雷斯海峽摩爾島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Marriage Customs and Star Myths — The Origin of the Tagai Constellation'

summary.en: Tagai the captain speared fish from the bow while Kareg poled the canoe through the reef; the hot sun made the crew thirsty, and they drank the ship's water-bamboo dry. Tagai made a rope fast round the necks of six men and cast them into the sea — 'All you fellow Usiam' — then killed the rest with two wooden skewers through their necks and called them Seg; only Kareg, who never stole his water, was spared, and Tagai and Kareg and canoe stop in one place, Usiam in another, and Seg in another — the sky's almanack of yam and turtle seasons.
summary.zh: 船長塔蓋立於船首叉魚，卡雷格在船尾撐篙過礁。烈日炙人，全體船員口渴難耐，偷飲了船長的竹筒飲水。塔蓋舉起空筒喝問『誰喝了水？』無人應答。他怒極，取繩套住六人的脖子拋入海中：『你們就是「烏西亞姆」！』又取兩支木針，把其餘水手一一殺死，以針穿頸拋海，名之『塞格』。唯卡雷格無過得生：『你留下，你不偷水，你一直撐船。』如今塔蓋、卡雷格與舟停於天上一處，烏西亞姆一處，塞格一處——這便是漁民與農夫的天曆：烏西�姆報新芋之期，塔蓋報海龜之汛，夜航則循塔蓋左手而行。

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, informant's own words); Meriam heritage of Torres Strait.

passages.text: A man named Tagai, with uplifted and outstretched hands bearing a spear, is supposed to stand upon a canoe, which is represented by the bowed row of stars that forms the scorpion's tail. Below the front end of the canoe is a single star, the anchor of the canoe, and near its other end is a red star that represents a man named Kareg. A cluster of stars is called Usiam, and another linear constellation is named Seg. Tagai is an important constellation, not only as an indication of the approach of certain seasons, but also for navigation purposes. 'Usiam he vick for new yams.' 'Seg he vick next kind of yam.' 'Tagai he vuk for turtle season. Two hand he come first; all turtle go to islands to leeward (to the west), and they eat turtle first. By-and-by face belong Tagai he come up; Dauarle get turtle, and then all the rest of Murray Island.' In sailing by night from Erub (Darnley Island) to Mer (Murray Island) they steer for the left hand of Tagai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Marriage Customs and Star Myths' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: One man, Tagai, he got a canoe. Tagai he stop in forehead (the bow or front end of the canoe) and look out and spear fish. Kareg he stop in stern. Plenty men crew. They go over reef; Kareg he pole canoe. Tagai he spear fish. Sun hot on reef, all men thirsty, and steal water in canoe belong captain. Tagai say, 'Why you no pole canoe good? I no spear fish.' By-and-by he say, 'Where water-bamboo?' He take bamboo and shake it; it empty. 'Who drink water?' Men no talk. Tagai get wild. He get one rope and make fast round neck of six men and chuck into sea. He put name to them, 'All you fellow Usiam.' Tagai take two wooden skewers and call other men in canoe, and kill plenty, and stick the skewers through their necks and chuck them in the sea, and call them 'Seg.' Kareg he live. Tagai tell Kareg, 'You stop; you no steal my water, you push canoe all time.' Man stop in sky all the time. Tagai, Kareg, and canoe stop in one place, Usiam stop in another place, and Seg stop in another place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Origin of the Tagai Constellation' (1901), given in the informant's own words; not verbatim.

title.zh: 多蓋妖女梅塔科拉布與布

region.en: Boigu and Kerpai, Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽博伊古島與克爾派村（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Star Myths — A Dorgai Constellation'

summary.en: Digging mound-bird eggs on Boigu, Nadai pulled and pulled at what would not come — and dragged out of the ground a sleeping Dorgai, Metakorab, wearing great white cowries tied at her chin. Every village he ran to for help emptied itself at her terrible face; only at Kerpai did Bu stay in the bachelors' quarters, shoot her with pig-arrows, and kill her. Both are now in the sky — the Dorgai going first, continually followed by Bu: Altair the body, the stars each side her arms, and the cluster Bu, that belongs to the north-west monsoon and calls the dances.
summary.zh: 博伊古島的納代去掘塚雉的蛋，一連拔出幾枚拔不動的『蛋』——原來是多蓋妖女梅塔科拉布睡在土塚之下，頷下繫著幾枚大白寶螺。他嚇得魂飛，逃回村中呼眾殺妖；可是各村的武士一見妖面便棄械而逃，環島皆然。最後到克爾派村，眾人仍然跑了，唯有名喚布的男子留在單身漢屋裡，張弓搭上射豬用的利箭，一箭斃妖。如今二者皆在天上：多蓋在前，布緊隨其後——多蓋便是牛郎星（他們稱 gaum『身體』），兩側是她的雙臂，而布則是那一簇星。這組星座屬西北季風；『多蓋升起之時，正是跳舞之季。』

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, told in Mabuiag 1888); Torres Strait heritage.

passages.text: Once upon a time a man named Nadai, living on the Island of Boigu, went into the bush to collect the eggs of the mound-bird, a bird that lays its eggs in a great mound of earth which it scratches up with its strong feet. He found a large mound, and dug into it till he came to what he thought was an egg. He tried to pull it up, but it stuck fast; then he tried to get another, but neither would that come away. It so happened that a Dorgai named Metakorab was sleeping under the mound, and she was wearing several large white cowry shells, and it was these that Nadai was pulling at, mistaking them for eggs. Nadai at last caught hold of the shell, which was tied on to the Dorgai's chin, and giving a tremendous pull he dragged the Dorgai out of the ground. He was so terrified at her appearance, that he fled back to the village and called out to the inhabitants to arm themselves and kill the Dorgai, who was sure to follow after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'A Dorgai Constellation' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: By-and-by a fly came, and behind it came the Dorgai; but the men no sooner saw her terrible face than they threw down their weapons and ran away in a fright. Then Nadai went on to the next village, but the same thing happened again. So he went on all round the island, but it always happened as before. At last Nadai came to a village called Kerpai, on the north side of the island, and he begged the people to stand firm and attack the Dorgai. They armed themselves, but when the fly came, and after it the Dorgai, they all took to their heels, as the others had done before, with the exception of one man named Bu. He remained in the bachelors' quarters, and armed himself with a bow and with arrows that are used for shooting wild pigs. When the Dorgai arrived, Bu shot her and killed her. Both are now in the sky; the Dorgai going first, being continually followed by Bu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'A Dorgai Constellation' (1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Kabi and the House of the Sun

region.en: Dauan and Saibai, Torres Strait (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 托雷斯海峽道安島與賽拜島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901 (from Robert Bruce at Daru)

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'Star Myths — Sun, Moon, and Night'

summary.en: At Kadau all men yammed that Sun, Moon, and Night were all the same one; Kabi alone said No, and when the assembly threatened to kill him he set out in his canoe to find where the Sun stopped. The Sun carried Kabi's canoe in one hand like a boy's toy, entertained him with bananas, yams, taro, and coconuts, hitched a rope to his head and towed him home through three big waves — and when Kabi shook the rope loose before all the people, they believed: 'Sun, Moon, and Darkness each got their own work to do.'
summary.zh: 道安島卡道的村人閒談皆言『日、月、夜原是同一個』。唯卡比說：『瞎說！你們看：日出之時月即落；月升之時日即沉——分明是三個。』眾人惱怒欲殺他；卡比便說『明天我去日月夜所居之地，親眼看給你們』。他駕舟遠航，過賽拜、越大洋，果真尋到日之所居。太陽單手提起他的小舟，如孩童提玩具一般放上屋頂，又以大珠貝佩胸出迎，待以蕉、芋、薯、椰之宴。臨別，太陽以繩繫其頭，拖舟而行；三大浪相繼，一波送他半程，一波至賽拜，一波直送道安。他登岸對眾人說：『我去過日月之家——他們是兩個，不是一個。你們看這繩——』解繩之時，繩竟向天而去。眾人這才信了：『日、月、黑夜，各司其職。』

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901, from Robert Bruce at Daru); Torres Strait heritage.

passages.text: Plenty men sit down and yarn at Kadau (a village in the island of Dauan). All man he yarn about Sun, and Moon, and Night. All man speak, 'Sun, Moon, and Night he all the same one.' One man called Kabi he speak, 'No good you talk all the same; suppose you look. You see. Sun he come up, that time Moon he go down. Moon he come up, and Sun he go down.' Then all man too much wild; some man he speak, 'Very good, we kill Kabi; he talk no good.' Kabi he hear, he afraid. Kabi he then speak, 'You fellow, look, I go to-morrow; I go place belong Sun, and Moon, and Night.' At small daylight he go in his canoe, his woman stop behind. He go across to Saibai. All man in Saibai speak, 'Where you go, Kabi?' He speak, 'I go to look place where Sun he stop.' Him go — go — go. All islands he come up. He go big deep water. He catch him place where Sun he stop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kabi he look, Sun he come out house belong him. Kabi he think, 'Sun he no good, as Sun he no got good things on.' Kabi pulled his canoe on beach and sat down. Sun then come out of door of his house and looked at Kabi. Sun then go inside house belong him and put on all flash things — one big pearl-shell he put on breast and one big shell on body. Sun he walk along and come close to Kabi. Kabi he very much afraid; he think inside, 'Big man he come now. I think he kill me.' Sun he speak, 'Kabi, come on, you and me go house.' Sun he carry canoe belong Kabi in his one hand, all same as boy carry canoe belong play; then he put canoe on top of his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Sun he speak, 'Kabi, what name you come here for?' Kabi he speak, 'All man he growl for you; he all speak, Sun, and Moon, and Night he one. Me, one fellow, speak, No, Sun he one. Moon he one, and Night he one. Then all man he wild.' Sun he speak, 'All right, you come house.' Sun he speak, 'Me one, Moon another one.' Then Sun and Moon he bring Kabi kaikai (food). Sun he give kaikai belong Sun — bananas, yams, taro, sweet potatoes, coconuts. Moon he give him all the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sun he take canoe belong Kabi, and put it in the water; then they put all kaikai in canoe. Kabi he get afraid when he think of the long journey he got to take. Sun he speak, 'Kabi, I make rope fast along your head, then you and me go together; I tow you. When you come to place belong you, you shake rope; by-and-by when you loose rope, you shake it, then that time I pull up.' Kabi he then start in his canoe. Three big waves come; one wave lift him half-way, the next lift him along to Saibai, the next wave lift his canoe to Dauan. Kabi then went ashore and told all the people, 'I been to place where Sun and Moon he stop. You hear me now when I speak. He no one fellow, he two fellow. Sun he pull me here.' Then Kabi got all people in one place. He speak, 'You see this rope fast on top of my head. You look when I take this rope off my head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'Sun, Moon, and Night' (1901), from Robert Bruce; not verbatim.

title.en: Kwoiam of Mabuiag, the Berserker of the Straits
title.zh: 馬布瓦格狂戰士克沃伊亞姆

region.zh: 托雷斯海峽馬布瓦格島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown, 1901

source.work: A. C. Haddon, Head-Hunters Black, White and Brown (London: Methuen, 1901), 'The Cult of Kwoiam'

summary.en: Cursed by his blind mother for a stolen strip of plaiting-leaf, Kwoiam killed her and went on the rampage 'to pay for mother,' returning with a canoe-load of heads; he slew whole villages and every expedition sent against him until his throwing-stick broke, and he backed slowly up his hill and crouched and gave up the ghost. 'No cut him head; he great man' — his foes heaped their weapons over him, and the cairn on Kwoiam's hill still carries three shell trumpets, while the spring his spear drove into the rock flows yet, its upper pool forbidden to the unworthy, whose penalty is premature grey-ness.
summary.zh: 克沃伊亞姆與盲母同住，舅父為其隨從。一日他以腳趾抽走母親編席的一片葉，受母咒罵；他怒而出門，取椰芽飾身，竟弒母，繼而『為母償血』，掀起殺伐：先屠數島，直上新幾內亞大陸，歸來載回一舟頭顱。巴杜人拒他魚食戲弄於他，他追至普魯島午寢之地盡殲之。兩批復仇大軍皆被誅盡；至第三批，他的擲矛杆折斷，手無寸鐵的他且戰且退，退上山頂，俯身而亡。敵方一名巴杜勇士喝止行刑者：『莫砍他的頭！他是偉人，讓他躺在這裡——他是這些島嶼的主人。』敵人反以弓箭矛棒為其堆塚。今日克沃伊亞姆崗上石塚猶存，塚置三枚古貝號。岩隙中他那矛鑿出的泉水至今長流：上池唯老者尊者可飲，僭飲者必早生華髮。

sensitivity.note: Field record (Haddon 1901); Kwoiam cult heritage of Mabuiag. Records head-hunting warfare as remembered history.

passages.text: Kwoiam lived with his mother, who was blind, and he had an uncle for his henchman. One day, when his mother was plaiting a mat, Kwoiam abstracted with his toes a strip of leaf his mother was about to use, and missing it she asked who had taken it. Kwoiam confessed, and his mother cursed him; this made him angry, and he went outside the hut and called to his uncle to get the sprouting leaf of a coconut palm that he might deck himself for the war-path. When he was so accoutred he killed his mother, and then went on the rampage to avenge her death, or as it was told to me, 'to pay for mother.' He went to several islands and to the mainland of New Guinea, sometimes slaying the population of a whole village, at other times merely requesting food or a new canoe. Eventually Kwoiam returned with a canoe-load of human heads, and he ordered his uncle to clean them for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: On one occasion certain Badu men fooled him, refusing to give him some fish for which he had civilly asked them. These men retired to the island of Pulu for a midday siesta; Kwoiam followed them there and killed them all except two, who made their escape, but one of them had his leg transfixed by a javelin hurled by Kwoiam. An expedition of Moa and Badu men was sent to retaliate; but Kwoiam killed all who were sent against him except four men. A second very large avenging expedition was sent, but when fighting against these Kwoiam's throwing-stick broke, and he was helpless. He slowly retreated backwards up his hill, and when the enemy pressed too closely upon him, he rushed forward, unarmed as he was, and frightened back his foes; this happened several times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as Kwoiam reached the summit of the hill he crouched in a prone position and gave up the ghost. A Moa man rushed up to him and began to cut off his head with a bamboo knife, but he had only made a small incision when he was stopped by another Badu man, who said, 'No cut him head; he great man. Let him lie where he stop; he master over all these islands.' So instead of insulting the dead warrior they did him honour, and piled over his body their bows, arrows, javelins, and stone clubs, saying that now Kwoiam was dead all the fighting was over. The cairn erected over his grave remains to this day, and on it are placed three ancient shell trumpets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the plain near the sea is a large oval boulder, the head of the luckless mother. As we ascended the hill called Kwoiamantra we passed between a long double row of stones that represented the heads taken by Kwoiam on the famous voyage when he paid the blood-price for the death of his mother. A short distance up the hill were some rocks, from out of a cleft in which a perennial stream flows. It arose in this wise. One day Kwoiam was thirsty, and he drove his spear into the rock, and water gushed forth and has never ceased to flow. The water fills a rock basin, and from this it trickles into a lower pool, and thence the stream flows down the hill. Ten years before I was informed that only old and important men might drink from the upper pool, whereas the lower was free to all; the penalty of unworthily drinking from the upper pool was premature greyness. I asked if I might drink there, and they were good enough to think that my claims were sufficiently strong. Apparently I was presumptuous, as the penalty has been inflicted!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Haddon, Head-Hunters, 'The Cult of Kwoiam' (1901); not verbatim.
